name: Ariel Hernandez
zh_summary: RealSimpleAriel 強調時機大於位置，研究日線圖和劇本，如支撐缺口、6/20、VWAP 收回、ORB、前日高點突破等設置。
text:
WHEN > WHERE

So many people want to fight for pennies on a big-picture trade idea.

When you take the time to study the daily chart and understand your playbook, whether you’re buying a support gap, a 6/20 setup, a VWAP reclaim, a 5-minute ORB or a break of the prior day’s high, these are relatively small nuances in the grand scheme of things.

Yes, I’m aware that certain entries allow for tighter risk management and potentially larger position sizes.

BUT, and this is the more important part, are you recognizing what is going on around you that would create the conditions necessary for your trade idea to actually work?

Over time, you’ll come to learn that WHEN you buy something is far more important than WHERE you bought it.

Show up to buy $SMH or $GLD after 10 a.m. today and you’re likely making money regardless of which entry technique you employed. But show up to buy those same names 2, 4 or 10 days ago, and you could have been getting destroyed because you failed to recognize that it wasn’t the proper “WHEN.”

You can have a textbook entry in the wrong environment and still lose money. Conversely, you can have a mediocre entry in the right environment and make a lot of money.

Spend more time studying the conditions that make your setups work and less time obsessing over the perfect entry.

Something to stew on over the holiday weekend. 🦃

Pricing talk is a 7% to 7.5% yield, while CoreWeave's 2031 bonds were yielding close to 18% this morning, per Tradeweb data.

Why it matters: this morning's story was CoreWeave's credit getting priced like distress. This is the other side of the neocloud model. The company's credit is weak, but Meta's is strong, and lenders are lending against the customer, not the borrower. With about $46.9B of debt on the balance sheet at the end of September, CoreWeave needs that door to stay open. If this prices near the talk, the GPU orders for Georgia keep moving. text:
Taiwan Semiconductor $TSM and the AI hardware chain got a big carve out in Washington's new tariff push: chips, servers, server boards, network switches and chipmaking tools are all on the exemption list.

USTR on Wednesday proposed Section 301 tariffs on 14 economies over what it calls "structural excess capacity." Taiwan and Korea each face up to 15% including normal duties, with a fallback of up to 25% if USTR decides ongoing talks fall short. Malaysia is up to 18%, China up to 20% and Vietnam up to 35%. Mexico got no determination for now.

The fine print is the story for AI. Semiconductor articles are exempt because they already sit under the Section 232 chip tariffs, and the Taiwan, Korea and Malaysia annexes also exclude computers and processing units (the server codes), their circuit board assemblies, switching and routing gear, and semiconductor manufacturing equipment. USTR still calls out Taiwan's support for high tech manufacturing and warns that over reliance on a single economy for semiconductors "increases the cost of any disruption."

Chips are getting crushed today anyway, with the selloff tied to AI spending doubts, the tariff headlines and rising Fed hike bets. My read: these proposals are not a direct hit on AI data center hardware. Nothing is final yet, and the proposals are open for public comment into January.

text:
SpaceX $SPCX just got the first US license ever for a full constellation of data centers in space: the FCC authorized up to 1 million "Starmind" orbital compute satellites.

The order comes with hard deadlines. SpaceX needs one satellite operating by Nov. 25, 2033, 10% of the fleet by 2035, 50% by 2038 and all of it by 2040, or the authorization goes void. The satellites fly in shells from 500 to 1,002 km, move data over laser links into Starlink, and only get Ka-band radio as a backup. The FCC also denied petitions to block it from Amazon's Kuiper, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society.

"By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment," FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said.

The fine print: the debris plan was only approved for satellites below 600 km. SpaceX's request to dispose of higher satellites without burning them up in the atmosphere was deferred, so anything above 600 km needs another filing first. And a license is not a launch. The first deadline is still seven years out.

Why it matters: on Earth, data centers are stuck waiting on power, land and permits. text:
Ray Dalio says investors mistake great technology for a great investment in a bubble and compares the AI boom with the innovations of the 1920s

“A lot of people think a bubble is whether the price gets beyond that which can come from the present value of future cash flows, and that’s not it, because what happens is you don’t know the future cash flows for decades, let’s say, if you take the present value.

“In any case, even those with good financial cash flows have had bubbles. So you could see the 1920s bubbles, and then you have the collapses. Even if they work out in the long run, you have the bubble bursting.

“The bubble, the mechanics of it, is that people mistake a great new technology for a great investment.

“In the ’20s, imagine what that was like. That was the first time you had electricity in houses, so you had lighting and you had refrigeration. You had movies, you had radio, you had cars, you had airplanes—all of this new technology coming on. It would be more apparent than anything we’ve seen even with AI.”

@NaveenGRao sold Nervana to Intel and MosaicML to Databricks. His third company, @unconvai, is building something that looks nothing like a GPU.

text:
Some takeaways from this report.

$60B of new AI orders in 13 weeks. $132B backlog. Full year raised by $10B. And every order "rigorously vetted for customer quality and access to capital, land and power." That's Dell directly answering the circular financing fear. Demand strong enough that you can turn away unvetted buyers is not what a bubble top looks like.

Q4 EPS guides down sequentially on rising component costs, and inventory nearly tripled to feed the backlog. Great quarter, tougher margin road ahead.

Bigger picture, Dell is the backbone of this buildout. They assemble the racks, test them, and stand them up. 

The backbone says demand is accelerating across 7,500+ customers, so everything downstream of those racks eventually gets its piece. Connectivity, power, cooling, all of it.
